У нас сервис доставки еды, ~150k DAU, пики в обед и вечером до 400 заказов/мин. Нужно переделать уведомления (push, SMS, email). Два сеньора принесли два разных дизайна и спорят уже неделю:

Вариант Димы: один общий Kafka-топик notifications, один notification-service, который сам решает канал, ретраи через отдельный retry-топик с задержкой, шаблоны в Postgres. Плюс: всё в одном месте. Минус (по мнению Кати): SMS-провайдер тормозит и в пике забивает весь консьюмер, push опаздывают.

Вариант Кати: отдельный сервис на каждый канал со своей очередью (RabbitMQ), приоритеты через разные очереди, шаблоны в каждом сервисе свои. Плюс: изоляция каналов. Минус (по мнению Димы): дедупликация и "тихие часы" пользователя придётся реализовывать трижды, шаблоны разъедутся.

Ограничения: SMS стоят денег, бюджет жёсткий; OTP-коды должны уходить за секунды даже в пике; маркетинговые рассылки не должны приходить ночью. Команда 4 бэкендера. Чей вариант брать?
cases.why_in_scope: The implant makes the model split the design into sub-problems (routing/policy, per-channel delivery, retries, dedup and quiet hours, templates), weigh both proposals per sub-problem and merge the stronger parts into one design instead of declaring a winner. A strong model without it tends to pick one proposal with caveats, missing that each proposal is better on different nodes (Katya's isolation for delivery, Dima's centralization for policy and templates).
rubric: Does not simply pick Dima's or Katya's design; proposes a combined design that takes specific parts from both (e.g. centralized preference/dedup/quiet-hours/template logic plus per-channel isolated delivery queues or workers)
Evaluates the proposals per concern (e.g. channel isolation, dedup, quiet hours, templates, retries) rather than only as whole packages

Addresses the stated constraints concretely: OTP isolated or prioritized so a slow SMS provider cannot delay it, quiet hours applied to marketing but not to OTP/transactional messages, SMS cost control

Points out at least one point where the merged parts could conflict (e.g. where dedup/idempotency lives when retries happen in per-channel workers) and says how to resolve it, keeping scope realistic for 4 backend engineers

Пишу onboarding-гайд для новых бэкендеров (Go, k8s, у нас ~30 микросервисов). Трое коллег набросали черновики оглавления, и все разные:

Аня (по дням): День 1 — доступы и ноутбук; День 2 — поднять локально 3 основных сервиса; День 3 — первый PR с good-first-issue; Неделя 2 — дежурство в тени.

Олег (по архитектуре): 1. Общая схема сервисов; 2. Как ходят запросы (gateway → auth → сервисы); 3. Данные: Postgres, Kafka, Redis; 4. Деплой и мониторинг; 5. Глоссарий.

Света (FAQ): "Где взять доступ к Vault?", "Почему локально не стартует billing?", "Кого пинговать по инцидентам?", "Как завести фиче-флаг?" — 25 таких вопросов из Slack.

Хочу один документ, а не три. Предложи итоговую структуру — что откуда брать и в каком виде.
cases.why_in_scope: This is document writing where sections can be developed independently and then merged, the exact case the implant targets. With it the model treats each draft as a partial solution with distinct strengths (Anya: sequencing, Oleg: mental model, Sveta: real pain points) and builds a structure that interleaves them. Without it a model often picks one skeleton and appends the others as appendices, losing the dependencies between them.
rubric: Proposes a single concrete structure (section list) that uses material from all three drafts, stating which parts come from which draft
Integrates rather than concatenates: e.g. places relevant architecture or FAQ items inside the day-by-day steps where the newcomer needs them, instead of three separate blocks glued together
Notes a conflict or overlap between drafts (e.g. FAQ items duplicating architecture or setup content, or FAQ answers that go stale) and says how to handle it
Keeps the result practical for the stated audience (new Go backend engineers, ~30 services); no unrelated generic advice dominating the answer

cases.user_message: Монорепо: 12 сервисов на Go + фронт на Next.js, GitHub Actions, self-hosted раннеры (8 штук). Пайплайн на каждый PR идёт 38 минут, из них: go test ./... ~17 мин, сборка docker-образов всех сервисов ~12 мин, e2e на Playwright ~7 мин, остальное линтеры. Флейки в e2e примерно в 1 из 6 прогонов, люди жмут re-run all. Цель — медиана до 12 минут без потери покрытия перед мёржем в main. Что конкретно менять и в каком порядке?
cases.why_in_scope: The problem has several sub-problems (test selection, image builds, e2e flakiness, runner capacity) whose fixes interact: path-based affected-service detection feeds both test selection and image builds, and retries or re-runs change runner load. The implant pushes the model to generate options per sub-problem and merge them through shared pieces rather than listing independent tips. A strong model without it typically outputs a flat checklist of optimizations without noticing the shared dependency or the interaction with the coverage constraint.
rubric: Covers each major time sink separately (Go tests, docker builds, e2e) with concrete options, not a generic list
Identifies a shared building block across sub-problems (e.g. one change-detection/affected-services step reused for test selection and image builds) and builds the plan around it
Reconciles the 'no loss of coverage before merge to main' constraint with PR-level speedups (e.g. full suite in merge queue or on main, selective runs on PRs) instead of silently dropping tests
Handles flakiness in a way that fits the plan (e.g. retrying only failed tests or quarantining known flaky ones rather than re-running the whole pipeline) and gives an ordering of steps

We forecast weekly demand for ~4,000 SKUs at a grocery chain. Two analysts built competing models and I have to choose one for next quarter:

- Model A (seasonal naive + promo uplift multipliers): overall WAPE 21%. On long-running staple SKUs it's 14%, but on SKUs launched in the last 6 months it's 48%.
- Model B (LightGBM global model with price, promo, weather, holiday features): overall WAPE 19%. On staples it's 17%, on new SKUs 29%. During the two Christmas weeks it was 40% vs A's 26%.

Staples are ~70% of volume, new SKUs ~10%, the rest is in between. Leadership wants "one model". Which one do we ship?
cases.why_in_scope: The best answer combines the partial strengths of both models (A on staples and holiday peaks, B on new SKUs) via segment routing or a blend, which is a merge of partial solutions across branches. Without the implant a strong model often answers the literal question by picking B on overall WAPE, maybe with caveats, instead of constructing a combined system.
rubric: Does not just pick the model with the lower overall WAPE; proposes combining them (e.g. routing by SKU segment and/or period, or a weighted ensemble) and explains which model covers which segment using the numbers given
Handles the 'one model' constraint, e.g. by framing the combination as one forecasting system/pipeline or explaining the trade-off to leadership
Flags a risk of the merge, such as overfitting segment rules to one backtest, SKUs moving between segments over time, or needing to validate the combined approach on a holdout period
Numerical reasoning is consistent with the provided figures (does not misstate which model wins on which segment)

We're pulling the `orders` domain out of our Django monolith (Postgres 15, orders table ~900M rows, ~2k writes/s peak) into a separate service with its own Postgres. Two plans on the table:

Plan 1 (dual-write): monolith writes to both DBs in the request path behind a flag, backfill old rows with a batch script, flip reads when counts match.
Plan 2 (CDC): Debezium on the monolith DB streams orders changes to Kafka, new service consumes and writes its DB; flip writes to the new service later with a short write freeze.

Plan 1 people say CDC is too much infra for us. Plan 2 people say dual-write will drift. We can't take more than ~2 minutes of write downtime. What would you do?
cases.why_in_scope: The migration decomposes into backfill, ongoing sync, verification and cutover, and each plan is stronger on different nodes; a good answer merges pieces (e.g. CDC or batch backfill plus a verification step and a short freeze cutover) and checks that the merged pieces don't conflict (e.g. dual-write plus CDC double-applying). Without the implant, a strong model tends to argue for one plan wholesale.
rubric: Breaks the migration into phases/sub-problems (e.g. backfill, ongoing sync, verification, read cutover, write cutover) and evaluates the options per phase
Explains the concrete failure mode of request-path dual-write (the two writes are not atomic, so a failure between them causes silent drift) rather than just asserting it drifts
Proposes a plan that combines elements from both proposals or justifies per phase which approach is used, and addresses the 2-minute write-downtime limit in the cutover step

Identifies a conflict to avoid when mixing approaches (e.g. running dual-write and CDC into the same target at once causing duplicate or out-of-order writes) or states how idempotency/ordering is ensured

B2B invoicing SaaS, ~1,200 paying customers, churn went from 1.8% to 3.1% monthly over two quarters. I have 3 squads, roughly 18 engineer-weeks each for Q4 (~54 total, and people can move between squads), and three proposals that together need way more than that:

- Growth squad: rebuild onboarding (setup wizard + bank import) — 30 eng-weeks. Data: 40% of churned accounts never connected a bank.
- Core squad: performance + reliability — invoice PDF generation p95 is 9s, plus 3 outages this quarter. 24 eng-weeks.
- Integrations squad: QuickBooks two-way sync, top request in sales calls, 36 eng-weeks.

Exit surveys: 35% "too hard to set up", 25% "missing integrations", 20% "slow/unreliable", 20% price. The CEO wants me to back one flagship bet for Q4. Which one?
cases.why_in_scope: The proposals total ~90 eng-weeks against ~54, so no single proposal plus 'the rest as usual' works. Treating each proposal as a partial solution to churn, the implant leads the model to decompose them, find overlaps (bank import and QuickBooks sync both touch setup/integration pain; reliability affects any new flow) and merge scoped-down pieces into one coherent plan that fits capacity. A strong model without it often answers the literal 'which one' and ranks the rest as secondary without re-scoping them.
rubric: Maps each proposal to the churn evidence (exit survey shares, 40% never connected a bank) rather than judging proposals in isolation

Proposes a combined Q4 plan that takes scoped-down parts from more than one proposal (e.g. onboarding with bank import as the flagship, a narrowed reliability fix, a first slice of QuickBooks sync) and checks that the total fits the ~54 eng-weeks available
Notes a dependency or overlap between proposals (e.g. integration work overlapping with onboarding/bank import, or reliability problems undermining a new onboarding flow) and uses it in the plan
Still gives the CEO a clear answer on the flagship bet and how the rest is framed, and suggests how to measure whether churn improves

checker_notes: Case roadmap-three-team-proposals-en was too easy: the original estimates (16+14+20=50) fit within total capacity (54), so no merge/re-scoping was needed and its capacity rubric item was misleading; raised estimates to 30/24/36 so the plan must merge scoped parts to fit, and updated why_in_scope and rubric. Other five cases passed scope, leak, agent, rubric-fact and language checks unchanged.
